draft.title: Arrhenius and Brønsted-Lowry definitions
card: An acid releases H⁺ ions in water. A base releases OH⁻ ions in water. These definitions only work for water solutions.
An acid is a proton donor. A base is a proton acceptor. A proton here means an H⁺ ion.
Brønsted-Lowry works beyond water, such as gases or other solvents. In NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, HCl donates a proton to NH₃, so HCl is the acid and NH₃ is the base.
A substance is an acid or a base by what it does in a reaction. In water, H⁺ is carried by water as H₃O⁺, so an acid donates its proton to a water molecule.
draft.remember: Arrhenius is about ions released in water. Brønsted-Lowry is about proton transfer.

a.q: In the reaction NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl, which substance is the Brønsted-Lowry base?
opts: NH₃, because it accepts a proton
HCl, because it donates a proton
NH₃, because it releases OH⁻ ions
HCl, because it accepts a proton
a.why: NH₃ gains a proton from HCl to form NH₄⁺, so it is a proton acceptor and a Brønsted-Lowry base. Releasing OH⁻ in water is the Arrhenius idea, and it does not apply here because there is no water.
a.clue: Which substance ends up with an extra proton?

b.q: Hydrogen chloride gas reacts with ammonia gas, with no water present. Why can the Arrhenius definitions not describe this reaction, while Brønsted-Lowry can?
opts: Arrhenius needs water, but Brønsted-Lowry does not
Arrhenius needs a gas, but Brønsted-Lowry needs a solid
Brønsted-Lowry needs water, but Arrhenius does not
Arrhenius covers only bases, Brønsted-Lowry only acids
b.why: Arrhenius defines acids and bases by the ions they release in water, so it cannot apply with no water present. Brønsted-Lowry looks only at whether a proton is transferred, which happens here. The option that says Brønsted-Lowry needs water is wrong because it swaps the two definitions.
b.clue: Look at what each definition needs in order to apply.

a.best: NH₃, because it accepts a proton

b.best: Arrhenius needs water, but Brønsted-Lowry does not
